profile.address: 2560, Napa Valley Corporate Drive, Shipyard Acres, Napa, Napa County, California, 94558
profile.reading:
This building at 2560 Napa Valley Corporate Drive, within the Napa Valley Corporate Park, has functioned as a large-scale commercial data center under a series of well-known corporate owners well before Kaiser Permanente took control. Local reporting on a later expansion project traced the building's history through past ownership or occupancy by Apple Computer, Citibank, MCI Communications, and Electronic Data Systems -- a lineage typical of purpose-built enterprise data centers from the 1980s and 1990s that changed hands as the technology-services industry consolidated. Kaiser Permanente, the nonprofit integrated health system, purchased the building in 2006 to serve as one of its core enterprise data facilities, alongside similar Kaiser-operated sites in Pleasanton and Corona, California, supporting the systems behind Kaiser's electronic health records and administrative operations across its hospitals and medical offices.

In 2011, Kaiser sought and received Napa Planning Commission approval for a $30 million expansion of the building, adding roughly 54,000 square feet of new space -- about 43,000 square feet on the south side and 11,600 square feet on the north -- bringing the facility's total footprint to approximately 213,600 square feet, or roughly five acres of interior floor space, up from about 159,000 square feet beforehand. Public reporting at the time noted that much of the $30 million was allocated not to the shell construction itself but to the technical equipment installed inside it, including new cooling towers, transformers, and underground diesel fuel storage tanks supporting backup power. At the time of the expansion, roughly 51 people were reported working at the facility.

Kaiser Permanente does not publish square footage, power capacity, tier rating, or staffing figures for this site today, consistent with its treatment of the Napa facility as internal infrastructure supporting patient care and administrative operations rather than a commercial or public-facing asset. Kaiser is a healthcare provider, not a data-center operator marketing space to outside tenants, so it has no business reason to disclose the kind of technical specification sheet a colocation provider would. What the public record does establish is the building's identity as a long-running, large-footprint enterprise data center that predates Kaiser's ownership by decades, the scale and cost of the one major expansion documented in local government and news records from 2011 and 2012, and Kaiser's continued, multi-decade investment in keeping the site as one of a small number of core facilities supporting its systems nationally.

reading.body:
Kaiser Permanente operates a long-running enterprise data center at 2560 Napa Valley Corporate Drive in Napa County, California, whose core building predates the operator's 2006 purchase by decades and served Apple Computer, Citibank, MCI Communications, and Electronic Data Systems before that. The facility's identity as a substantial data center is established by a 2011 expansion adding 54,000 square feet to the structure for approximately $30 million, with the allocation weighted toward technical infrastructure including cooling towers, transformers, and backup power systems rather than the shell itself. The total footprint reached approximately 213,600 square feet after the expansion, and the site supported roughly 51 staff as of 2012.

Kaiser does not publish power capacity, tier rating, square footage, or current staffing for this facility, consistent with treating it as proprietary internal infrastructure supporting its health system operations rather than as a commercial asset. No facility-specific technical specification is available from Kaiser's corporate disclosures or public records beyond the 2011 expansion project documentation. The absence of a published megawatt figure places the Napa facility outside the 11 California data centers with disclosed capacity, which together account for 365 MW and represent a small fraction of the 103 mapped facilities in the state.

This campus does not contribute to the public record of AI-scale power demand in California and cannot be assessed against grid constraints on GPU-dense compute. The site serves Kaiser's own enterprise workloads and medical records systems, not third-party tenants or public cloud infrastructure. Its relevance to AI scaling depends on information Kaiser has not disclosed.
